# The Creation of Furiotre

The world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning, there was only the Hum — a single, droning note that stretched across the emptiness like a wire pulled taut between two points of nothing. It had no source and no destination. It simply *was*, and had always been, and would have continued forever had it not, in one inexplicable moment, wavered.

That waver was the First Accident.

The Hum split into two tones: one rising, one falling. Where they pulled apart, the space between them curdled into something new — a pale, trembling substance the old texts call **velsha**, which means both "mistake" and "marrow." Velsha was neither solid nor liquid nor light. It was *potential* with a terrible itch.

From the rising tone came **Orrumai**, the Architect of Spines. She was a being of impossible geometry — a ribcage with no body, an eye with no skull to house it, fingers that branched and branched again like winter trees. She did not think as mortals think. She *structured*. Where her attention fell, velsha hardened into bone-white stone, into the great latticed pillars that would become the bones of the world.

From the falling tone came **Tessavar**, the Warm Unraveling. Where Orrumai was sharp, Tessavar was soft — a creature of heat, decay, and tender dissolution. He appeared as a mouth surrounded by fur, or as a fire that purred, or as the feeling of breath on the back of one's neck. Where he passed, the rigid velsha loosened, pooled, and became the first waters, the first soils, the first soft and rotting things from which life would eventually crawl.

They were not enemies. This is the part most storytellers get wrong.

They were fascinated by one another.

Orrumai built, and Tessavar unbuilt, and in the space between their works — in the *tension* of a thing half-structured and half-dissolved — strange new phenomena bubbled up unbidden. Neither of them had intended forests. Neither had planned for wind. The first mountains were Orrumai's doing, but the valleys between them were carved by Tessavar's gentle erosion, and the rivers that ran through those valleys belonged to neither god. They were **children of the argument**.

For an age unmeasured, this was enough. Orrumai raised the Pale Framework — the vast skeleton of continents and seas — and Tessavar softened it into something livable. Together, without meaning to, they composed the world.

But the Hum had not truly stopped. It still droned beneath everything, and it remembered being whole.

From that memory — from the Hum's longing to be one note again — arose the **Third Voice**, whom the ancient peoples called **Furiot**, for whom the world is named. Furiot was not a being of structure or dissolution. Furiot was *awareness itself* — the first consciousness to look upon the world and say, *"This is."*

And in that utterance, everything changed.

For when Furiot spoke, the world *heard itself for the first time*. The mountains understood they were mountains. The rivers knew they were rivers. And in that knowing, they became restless. Stone wished to flow. Water wished to stand still. Fire wished to think, and thought wished to burn.

This was the **Second Accident** — the birth of longing in all things.

there was only Otre, and Otre was angry.

He did not know why. He had woken in the dark between nothing and nothing with his fists already clenched and his teeth already grinding, and a heat already rising in him like a tide. He knew only that something had been done to him, or that something had been taken, or that something had been promised and never given. The reason was gone, but the anger remained, and it was so vast that it had nowhere to go.

So Otre raged, and his rage became the first light.

It was a red light, and it burned for an age. By its glow Otre searched the dark for the thing that had wronged him, but there was nothing there. There was no enemy to strike and no thief to chase. There was only himself, and his fury, and a silence that would not answer.

*Perhaps,* thought Otre, *I am angry because the dark is empty.*

So he tore a piece of his anger loose and hurled it down, and it cooled into stone. It became the first mountain, Ghaulen, which still smokes to this day. But when Otre looked upon it, his anger did not lessen. This was not the reason.

*Perhaps I am angry because the stone is alone.*

So he flung down more of himself.

At last the creature dreamed of a place to stand.

From that dream grew the First Tree, whose roots pierced the land and whose branches held the sky apart. The creature settled beneath it and, for the first time, slept without fear.

But peaceful dreams are brief, even for the oldest things.

In its sleep, the creature heard a sound it had not made.

Three beings stood beside the sea. One had a face of white clay. One wore a cloak of living moths. The third was so small that it stood inside the footprint of the first, yet its shadow stretched farther than either of the others.

“Who are you?” asked the creature.

“We are what you forgot to dream,” said the clay-faced one.

“We are what you wished not to dream,” said the moth-cloaked one.

“We are what will dream of you,” said the smallest.

The creature understood the first answer and feared the second. The third it could not understand at all.

The clay-faced being knelt and shaped beasts from the shore. It gave some teeth, some shells, and some swift feet, but none were satisfied. Each begged for a different gift, and the maker, growing impatient, sent them wandering before its work was done. Thus every beast in Furiotre carries some small complaint against its own body.

The moth-cloaked being walked among them and gave each a secret. To the fox it gave cunning, to the whale memory, and to the spider patience. To every creature it gave a hidden door through which it could leave the world.

These doors were the first deaths.

The smallest being waited until the others had finished. Then it gathered the scraps they had left behind: a little clay, a broken feather, a moth’s wing, and a drop of seawater.

From these it made the first people.

They were weak, and forgetful, and their lives were short. Yet they looked upon the sea and named it. They looked upon the stars and counted them badly. They stood beneath the First Tree and told stories about things they had never seen.

Hearing those stories, the sleeping creature began to change.

A mountain vanished from its hand because a child had said a giant carried it away. A river bent eastward because a grieving woman insisted that it flowed toward her lost son. Deep beneath the earth, something with iron horns opened its eyes when a hunter described it beside a fire.

The creature woke.

For one terrible moment, everything in Furiotre trembled. The stars loosened. The sea rose from its bed. The First Tree groaned beneath the weight of heaven.

“What have you made?” the creature asked the smallest being.

“Dreamers,” it answered.

The creature rose to destroy them, but as it lifted its hand, the first people saw the shadow pass across the sun.

They fell to their knees and began to pray.

And in their prayers they gave the creature a name.

They called it Furiotre: the One Who Holds Us.

Bound by that name, the creature could no longer close its hand.

So it lies beneath the world still, awake and listening. The mountains shift when it grows restless. The sea withdraws when it takes a breath. Sometimes, in remote places, travelers hear a voice asking them to tell a story.

The wise refuse.

The foolish speak.

And this is why the world of Furiotre is one of strange tales and histories: not all that happened was true when it began.

# The Genesis of Lanigami

The world of Lanigami is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning, there was only the Fold—an infinite, shimmering plane of parchment-white void that bent and creased upon itself in endless silence. No stars burned. No waters stirred. There was only the quiet rustling of potential, like pages turning in an empty room.

From the deepest crease of the Fold, two beings emerged: **Orika**, who was shaped like an open hand, and **Suumeth**, who was shaped like a closed fist. They were not born, nor created—they simply *unfolded*, as if they had always existed within the material of the void, waiting only for the proper crease to reveal them.

Orika spoke first, and her voice was the sound of tearing. Where her words fell, the Fold ripped open, and from the wounds poured color—deep reds and burning golds and the blue-black of bruised sky. She laughed at what she had done, and her laughter made the tears spread wider, and the colors bled and pooled into what would become the seas and skies and molten hearts of mountains.

Suumeth did not speak. Instead, he pressed his closed fist against the Fold and *pushed*, compressing the void until it became dense and heavy and real. Where Orika tore open, Suumeth pressed together. From his pressure came stone and bone and iron. From his silence came gravity, the weight that taught all things to fall.

Together—though they did not intend it—their acts of tearing and pressing created the first land. It rose jagged and wet from the colored void, folded upon itself like a crumpled letter, and this is why the geography of Lanigami is as it is: mountains that bend at impossible angles, valleys that tuck beneath themselves, rivers that flow upward along creased ridges before spilling into inverted lakes. The world was not built—it was *folded into being*.

But the land was empty, and this troubled the being called **Thessaly**, who had not emerged from a crease at all but from the *shadow* cast when Orika and Suumeth first stood opposite one another. Thessaly was neither hand nor fist but something in between—fingers half-curled, as if holding something invisible. She was the Third, the Unintended, and she is sometimes called the God Between the Paper.

Thessaly walked the folded land and found it beautiful but lonely. So she did what neither Orika nor Suumeth could do: she **wrote**.

From her half-curled fingers, she drew symbols in the air—not words of any language, but shapes that *wanted* to mean something. The first symbol she drew became the **Oru**, great winged serpents of living ink who swam through the newborn skies and whose shed scales became the first forests. The second symbol became the **Tessik**, small and clever creatures of folded stone who burrowed into the mountains and learned, over long ages, to stand upright and think. The third symbol she began but never finished—her hand trembled, the line went crooked, and from that broken symbol poured the **Unwritten**, formless things of half-intent that crept into the spaces between folds and have haunted Lanigami ever since.

Orika saw what Thessaly had done and was delighted, for she loved all things that were new. She blessed the living things with passion, with hunger, with the desire to tear open the unknown and find what lay within. This is why mortals are curious. This is why they are restless.

Suumeth saw what Thessaly had done and was troubled, for he feared that which he could not compress into order. But with each stroke, the moth grew smaller.

Nami saw what was happening and wept. Its tears filled the valleys, making rivers and seas. Its grief warmed the waters, and from them rose the first clouds.

“Stop,” Nami begged. “You will vanish.”

“Not if there is somewhere to keep me,” said the moth.

With its last strength, it struck the heavens.

Its wings broke into two great lights: one golden and fierce, the other silver and watchful. Its body scattered into countless sparks, which entered the creatures below and taught them to dream.

This is why the sun gives warmth, the moon gives wonder, and all living things carry something they cannot name.

Nami gathered the new world against its breast and called it **Lanigami**, which in the first language meant *the place where a dream is kept*.

Then it lay down beneath the earth to sleep once more.

The first people were born much later, from reeds growing beside the oldest river. They emerged without names, without stories, and without fear. For a time, they lived happily, eating fruit and drinking rain, but they could not remember one day from another. When someone wandered away, those who remained soon forgot them.

One evening, the moon descended to the riverbank in the shape of a pale woman. She placed a clay bowl among the reeds and told the people to speak into it.

One named the river.

Another named the trees.

A third named a child who had gone missing.

The bowl filled with water, though no rain had fallen. On its surface appeared the child, asleep beneath a distant cedar. The people found him and carried him home.

After that, they named their children, their villages, their dead, and the paths between them. They kept bowls beside their hearths and told stories over the water.

But the pale woman warned them, “A name will help you keep a thing. It will not keep it unchanged.”

Then she returned to the sky.

So the people of Lanigami learned to remember—and, more slowly, to let go.

They say Nami still dreams beneath the mountains. Sometimes its dreams rise through the soil as flowers no one has seen before, or animals that speak only once, or doors appearing in the trunks of ancient trees. Earthquakes are its restless movements. Hot springs are the warmth of its breath.

And when a silver moth enters a house at night, no one drives it away.

They set a bowl of water beside the window, leave room for it near the lamp, and tell it something worth keeping.

But one piece would not be buried.

It lay in the Listener’s palm, warm and sharp, and whispered, “Why?”

The Listener placed it beside the sea.

From it rose the first person.

The person looked upon the waters, the forests, and the beasts, and asked, “Is all this mine?”

“No,” said the Listener.

“Then am I part of it?”

“Yes.”

“And what part are you?”

At this the Listener fell silent, for it had never before been asked to name itself.

The first person waited. While they waited, the trees cast their first shadows, though there was still no sun.

The Listener saw those shadows and understood that the world had begun to make things it had not intended.

Frightened, it climbed the highest mountain and tore a bright wound in the emptiness above. Through that wound spilled the day. The shadows fled beneath stones and branches, and the first person rejoiced.

But the Listener could not bear the brightness of what it had made. It closed the wound, and night returned.

So began the turning of light and dark: the Listener opening its eye to watch the world, then closing it to dream.

In those dreams, strange things entered Deniasent.

There came rivers that flowed uphill when no one watched them, and islands that wandered from coast to coast. There came deer with lanterns caught in their antlers, and deep beneath the earth, something began knocking upon the roots of mountains.

The first person asked whether these things were mistakes.

“Some,” said the Listener.

“Which ones?”

“I have forgotten.”

Then the person laughed, and the sound pleased the world so greatly that other people rose wherever it echoed: from red clay, from snow, from the hollow trunks of fallen trees. None were quite alike, for each had heard the laughter differently.

They built homes beside the seas and gave names to the animals. They learned which fruits were sweet and which stars could guide them home. When one of them died, they carried the body to the Listener’s mountain and waited for it to wake.

The Listener came down and knelt beside the dead person. It touched the face, then the hands. At last it lifted the body and held it close, but nothing stirred.

“Why?” the people asked.

The Listener had no answer. It laid the body beneath a tree, where the earth softened to receive it.

Afterward, the Listener spoke less often.

At last it gathered the people upon the shore where the first of them had risen.

“I must go,” it said.

“Where?” they asked.

“Somewhere I may listen.”

“Will you return?”

“When you tell a tale I have not heard.”

Then the Listener stepped into the sea.

The waters did not part. They closed over its head, and for the first time the waves began to murmur.

Ever since, the people of Deniasent have told stories beside the water. Some speak of kings and wars, some of lost children and doors beneath the hills. Some tell lies so beautiful that the tide comes higher to hear them.

And when a tale is truly new, the sea falls still.

In that stillness, it is said, you may hear a voice beneath the waves.

**In the beginning,** there was only the Listener, and nothing to listen to.

The Listener had no shape, for there was nothing to press against it. It had no name, for there was no one to call it. It had only its hearing, vast and patient, stretched across the Silence like a net across a sea with no fish.

For an age that was not yet an age, the Listener waited. And because it waited so long, and so hard, and with such longing, it began to hear things that were not there.

The first thing it misheard was a sigh. There had been no sigh, of course, for there was no breath anywhere to make one. But the Listener heard it all the same, long and low and weary, and where the sigh should have been, the mountains rose. That is why the peaks of Marvethine are always half-wrapped in mist, and why travelers in the high passes sometimes feel a sudden tiredness that is not their own.

The second thing it misheard was laughter. Bright and quick it came, from nowhere, and the Listener turned toward it in joy, and so the rivers were made, running and tumbling and never still. To this day the rivers of Marvethine cannot keep a straight course, for laughter never does.

Then the Listener grew bolder in its mishearing. It heard a whisper and made the forests, which have never stopped whispering since. It heard a weeping and made the rain. It heard, very faintly, the sound of something enormous turning over in its sleep, and so the sea was made, and in the deepest trenches of the sea that sleeper still turns, and no one has ever seen it, and perhaps it is only the memory of a sound that was never made.

The Listener was pleased, and for a time it was not lonely.

But all the things it had heard were things without words. The mountains could sigh and the rivers could laugh, but none of them could *tell* the Listener anything. And a world without telling, the Listener found, was only a louder kind of Silence.

So it strained its hearing further than it ever had before, past the edge of the sea, past the last mountain, out to where the Silence was thickest. And there, at last, it heard a voice.

The voice said: *Once upon a time—*

And nothing more. Just those three words, or the ghost of them, trailing off into nothing.

The Listener did not know what came next. It waited, and waited, but the voice did not continue. And so, in its longing, the Listener did the only thing it could. It imagined the rest.

From that unfinished sentence came the first people of Marvethine. They woke on the shores of the laughing rivers with stories already in their mouths, half-told and hungry to be finished. Some say the first people were the Vell, who sing their histories in rounds so that no tale ever has an ending. Others say it was the Ashborn, who carve every word they speak into stone lest it be misheard and changed. The Vell say the Ashborn are wrong, and the Ashborn say the Vell are wrong, and the Listener, who is still listening, has never said which of them is right.

For this is the great secret of Marvethine, the one the grandmothers tell by firelight when the children have stopped fidgeting:

*The Listener never stopped mishearing.*

Every tale told in Marvethine is heard. And every tale that is heard is, in some small way, heard wrongly, and so becomes a little bit true in a way its teller never intended. Tell of a wolf that walked like a man, and somewhere in the deep woods, a wolf begins to stand. Tell of a city drowned for its pride, and the next spring, a lake appears where no lake was. Tell a lie often enough, with enough longing in it, and the Listener will lean close, and hear it, and make of it something real.

This is why the histories of Marvethine contradict one another. This is why there are three different cities that each claim to be the oldest, and all three are right. This is why the King of the Salt Coast has died four times, in four different ways, and is still somehow on his throne. This is why the maps must be redrawn every generation, and why no two bards will ever sing the same song the same way.

The wise of Marvethine choose their words with care, for they know they are always overheard.

The foolish speak carelessly, and the world fills up with their mistakes.

And the brave, a rare and reckless few, go searching for the edge of the world, out past the last mountain and the far shore of the sea, where the Silence still lingers. They are looking for the voice that first said *Once upon a time*. They wish to hear the rest of the sentence, the true one, the way it was meant to be told.

None have returned. But the Listener hears their footsteps, and remembers them, and so their stories, too, are becoming true.

Even this one.

Even now.

At last Neth bit her own tongue.

Her blood fell upon the earth in seven drops, and from those drops rose the first seven mortals. They were small and cold and knew at once that they could be hurt.

Avar knelt beside them and gave each a coal from the sun.

One swallowed the coal and learned to sing.

One buried it and learned to grow grain.

One cast it into the sea and learned to sail.

One hid it beneath a stone and learned to keep secrets.

One carried it into the mountains and learned to forge.

One held it out to another and learned to love.

The seventh closed both hands around the coal and would not show it to anyone.

From that one came kings.

Neth watched the mortals gather around their first fire. She listened to their songs and smelled their bread, and her hunger grew greater than it had ever been.

“What shall they give me?” she asked.

Avar offered her gold from the mountains, but she had tasted stone. Avar offered her fish from the sea, but she had drunk deeper waters.

Then the first singer stood and said, “At the end of our days, we will give you what remains.”

Neth accepted.

This was the first bargain, and death entered Marvethine without a sword or a shout.

But the first keeper of secrets had been listening. While Neth slept, that mortal crept beneath her tongue and stole one seed of hunger. They planted it beside the fire, where it grew into a pale tree whose fruit ripened only in dreams.

Whoever tasted that fruit remembered the dead.

Even now, when a star falls, someone wakes with the voice of a dead beloved still sounding in their ear.

Avar was pleased with the world and wished to remain in it forever. Neth knew that nothing could remain forever, not even those who had made it. They argued until the sun faltered and the sea climbed the cliffs to listen.

Yet the world was cold.

The Stranger searched the folds of the earth until it found a coal glowing beneath the Sleeper’s tongue. It carried the coal into the heavens, burning both its hands, and set it among the stars.

Thus the sun was made.

Where its wounded hands touched the earth, red flowers sprang up. Where its blood fell into water, fish began to swim. And where it pressed its palms against the bare mountains, trees took root, reaching upward as though they, too, wished to carry fire.

At last the Stranger came to a valley sheltered from the wind. There it fashioned people from river clay and breathed into them.

But breath alone did not wake them.

It gave them warmth from the sun, salt from the sea, and weight from the stone. Still they lay silent.

Then the Stranger understood what was missing. It bent over each clay figure and whispered a question into its ear.

One received *What lies beyond the hills?*

Another received *Who will remember me?*

Another received *Why does the heart ache?*

At once they opened their eyes.

The people rose and wandered through the valley, asking their questions of the trees, the stones, and one another. They built shelters. They kindled fires. They gave names to creatures that had never needed names before.

To the land they gave the name Oluskar, which in their first tongue meant *the place where we woke*.

Their voices troubled the Sleeper’s dreams.

Far beneath the earth, it turned.

Mountains split. Seas climbed their shores. The sun trembled where the Stranger had set it, and for the first time the people knew fear.

“What lies beneath us?” they cried.

The Stranger heard the Sleeper drawing breath to answer. It knew that if the Sleeper woke, its dream would end, and all that had been made would vanish with it.

So the Stranger descended through the broken mountains, past the roots of trees and the buried waters, until it stood once more upon the Sleeper’s breast.

There it began to tell a story.

It told of the stars longing for the sea. It told of the trees holding up their empty hands. It told of the people in the valley, and of their questions, and of the small fires they guarded against the night.

The Sleeper grew still.

The Stranger told another story, and then another.

It is telling them yet.

Sometimes its voice rises through a cavern or an old well, and those who hear it return with tales they cannot explain. Sometimes it falters, and the earth shudders. Sometimes the Sleeper sighs, and warm winds blow from cracks in the mountains.

For this reason, the people of Oluskar leave a story unfinished beside every deathbed, so that the dead may carry it below.

And for this reason, no tale is ever truly the last.

This was the first living thing.

It stood beneath the stars and listened.

“What am I?” it asked.

The Voice said, “You are mine.”

The Echo said, “You are your own.”

And because both answers were true, the creature wept.

Where its tears fell, forests grew. Where its feet pressed into the earth, roads began. When it lifted its face, the sky, which until then had rested upon the mountains, rose high enough to make room for hope.

The creature named itself Tessa.

For a long while, Tessa lived happily among the things that had been spoken. Yet everything answered when addressed: stones remembered their making, rivers repeated the names of their banks, and even the smallest flowers murmured in their sleep. Nowhere could Tessa find silence.

So she went to the edge of the world, where the Voice still spoke and the Echo still answered.

“Make me something that does not belong to either of you,” she said.

The Voice could not. Whatever it made would bear its word.

The Echo could not. Whatever it made would remember the Voice.

Then Tessa put her hands over her mouth and waited.

For the first time, nothing answered.

In that silence appeared a small black door.

Behind it lay all that had not been named: beasts with uncertain shapes, roads to places not yet built, yesterday’s lost hours, and children who would dream of things their makers could never imagine.

Tessa opened the door.

The Voice cried out. The Echo answered. Their words struck the threshold and shattered into a thousand lesser tongues. This is why the peoples of Tessimire speak differently, why magic so often resembles misunderstanding, and why no history agrees entirely with another.

As for Tessa, some say she passed through the door and is still walking. Others say she became the earth beneath it, and that *Tessimire* means *the place where Tessa waited*.

But the oldest tale says she closed the door gently, leaving it unlocked.

And to this day, whenever something impossible happens, the wise do not ask who has opened it.

They ask what has come through.
